title: Inducible inferior-wall ischemia: right coronary artery (right-dominant circulation)
vignette: A 54-year-old man comes to the office due to episodic burning substernal chest pain. His pain increases with activity and improves with rest. The patient has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. His blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. Cardiac auscultation reveals a S4 heart sound. Lung and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. An ECG at rest shows left ventricular hypertrophy. A myocardial perfusion scan reveals inducible ischemia of the inferior surface of the heart. Which of the following coronary arteries is most likely occluded in this patient?

clues.text: burning substernal chest pain. His pain increases with activity and improves with rest
clues.note: Exertional substernal chest pain relieved by rest is stable angina from a flow-limiting coronary stenosis.

clues.text: inducible ischemia of the inferior surface of the heart
clues.note: The INFERIOR (diaphragmatic) wall of the left ventricle is supplied by the posterior descending artery, which in most people (right-dominant) arises from the RIGHT coronary artery.

whatMatters: The INFERIOR (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart is supplied by the POSTERIOR DESCENDING ARTERY, which in ~85-90% of people (RIGHT-DOMINANT circulation) arises from the RIGHT CORONARY ARTERY. So inducible inferior-wall ischemia points to RCA occlusion. Answer D.
strategy: Map the ischemic territory to its artery: inferior wall -> posterior descending artery -> RCA (right-dominant, most common). Reject arteries supplying other walls: LAD (anterior wall + anterior septum), left circumflex (lateral/posterolateral wall), left main (large anterior+lateral territory), and right marginal branch (RV free wall).

eliminations.label: LAD - anterior wall/septum
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the left anterior descending artery. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it supplies the ANTERIOR wall, anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum, and apex - not the inferior wall. ✅ Correct if: anterior/anteroseptal ischemia (V1-V4).

eliminations.label: Left circumflex - lateral/posterolateral wall
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the circumflex branch of the left coronary. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it supplies the LATERAL and posterosuperior LV wall; only in the ~10% left-dominant circulation does it give the PDA. ✅ Correct if: lateral-wall ischemia (I, aVL, V5-V6), or left-dominant inferior supply.

eliminations.label: Left main - large anterior+lateral territory
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the left main coronary (divides into LAD + circumflex). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: its occlusion causes extensive anterior+lateral ischemia, not isolated inferior-wall ischemia. ✅ Correct if: large anterolateral territory at risk.

eliminations.label: Right marginal branch - RV free wall
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an acute (right) marginal branch of the RCA supplying the right ventricular wall. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it supplies the RV, not the inferior LV surface (which is the PDA territory). ✅ Correct if: isolated RV involvement.

reasoning: Exertional angina with inducible inferior-wall ischemia on perfusion scan
The inferior (diaphragmatic) LV wall is supplied by the posterior descending artery
In most people (right-dominant, ~85-90%) the PDA arises from the right coronary artery
mechanism: The right and left main CORONARY ARTERIES arise from the aortic root. The LEFT MAIN divides into the LEFT ANTERIOR DESCENDING (LAD; anterior wall, anterior 2/3 of the septum, apex) and the LEFT CIRCUMFLEX (lateral and posterosuperior LV). The RIGHT CORONARY ARTERY (RCA) supplies the right atrium/ventricle (and, via nodal branches, the SA node in ~60% and AV node in ~90%). CORONARY DOMINANCE is defined by which artery gives off the POSTERIOR DESCENDING ARTERY (PDA): in ~85-90% of people the circulation is RIGHT-DOMINANT (PDA from the RCA), while ~10% are left-dominant (PDA from the circumflex). The PDA runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the posterior 1/3 of the septum and most of the INFERIOR (diaphragmatic) wall of the LV (formed mostly by the LV, partly by the RV). Therefore inducible ischemia of the INFERIOR surface, in a typical right-dominant patient, indicates occlusion of the RIGHT CORONARY ARTERY. The distractors supply the anterior (LAD), lateral (circumflex), large anterolateral (left main), or RV (right marginal) territories.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid CV/Anatomy > coronary territories: LAD (anterior wall/septum/apex), circumflex (lateral/posterolateral), RCA (RV, inferior wall via PDA in right-dominant ~85-90%, SA/AV nodes); dominance = source of PDA.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Inferior wall = PDA = RCA (right-dominant, most common).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on coronary dominance, posterior descending artery, inferior/diaphragmatic wall, or LAD/circumflex territories? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: LAD = anterior; circumflex = lateral (PDA only if left-dominant); left main = anterolateral; right marginal = RV.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: inferior-wall ischemia (II, III, aVF) = RCA (right-dominant PDA); watch for AV block/bradycardia.

keywords.back: Which artery gives off the posterior descending artery

memoryHook: The bottom (inferior) of the heart is fed by the posterior descending artery - and in most people that branch comes off the RIGHT coronary artery.
